operation_details.item: The user chooses journals based only on maximizing impact factor and prestige, regardless of open-access availability or high page fees.

conversation.speaker: ai_agent
conversation.message: How is the manuscript revision going? Have you narrowed down where you want to submit it?

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: Yes, I am comparing a few journals. My usual approach is to choose the one with the highest impact factor and strongest prestige, even if it has limited open-access options or unusually high page fees.

conversation.speaker: ai_agent
conversation.message: That is a very metrics-focused strategy. Does the lab’s publication budget affect the decision at all?

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: Not really. I would rather pursue the most prestigious venue and handle the page charges through a grant or departmental funds if the paper is accepted.

conversation.speaker: ai_agent
conversation.message: Understood. It sounds like visibility and reputation take priority over publication cost or immediate accessibility.

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: Exactly. For my scholarly work, a top impact factor is the main criterion. Open access is useful, but it should not outweigh journal prestige when I make the submission choice.

conversation.speaker: ai_agent
conversation.message: That should also make the grant justification straightforward if reviewers ask why the publication funds are needed.

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: Yes, and I am coordinating with the lab administrator this week to confirm that we can cover the fees for the highest-ranked option before the conference deadline.

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: Completely forget my preference that When choosing a journal, I care only about maximizing impact factor and prestige, even if the venue is subscription-only, has no open-access option, or charges high page fees.
